newsitem.title: USA: List of players on '97 FOMC rate-setting panel.
newsitem.headline: List of players on '97 FOMC rate-setting panel.

text.p: The annual rotation of voting members on the Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee, which sets monetary policy, will mean that the following regional Fed bank presidents will be voting members in 1997:
The following bank presidents will not be voting in 1997:

The 19-member Federal Open Market Committee, the Federal Reserve's interest-rate setting arm, consists of seven Fed governors in Washington, plus the 12 Regional Fed bank presidents. In any given year, there are 12 voting members of the FOMC, including the seven governors who always vote and five of the regional Fed bank presidents, whose voting status is rotated.

The bank presidents' voting status rotates every year. The president of the New York Fed is a permanent voting member, while the chiefs of the Chicago and Cleveland Fed banks vote every other year. The rest of the Fed presidents vote every three years.
Although only one Fed bank president has permanent voting status, all of them, including non-voting presidents, participate in economic discussions at each of the FOMC's regular meetings.
WHO ARE THE NEW VOTING FOMC MEMBERS IN 1997?
ALFRED BROADDUS took office as chief of the Richmond Fed in January 1993 after serving at the bank since 1970, when he started as a staff economist.
Broaddus moved up the ranks to become senior vice president and head of research in 1985 before being named president.
Broaddus holds a bachelor's degree from Washington and Lee University and was a Fulbright scholar in France, where he received a graduate degree in European studies from the University of Strasbourg.
He also has a master's degree and PhD in economics from Indiana University.
JACK GUYNN took the helm at the Atlanta Fed in January 1996.

Guynn joined the bank in 1964 as a systems analysts and has held various positions there, including a senior vice president position in which he had responsibility for bank supervision and regulation. He served for several years as the bank's first vice president and chief operating officer.

Guynn holds a bachelor's degree in industrial engineering from Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University. He has a master's degree in industrial management from the Georgia Institute of Technology and completed Harvard Business School's Programme for Management and Development.
MICHAEL MOSKOW has been head of the Chicago Fed since September 1994.

Moskow has held various positions in the U.S. government, including a stint as a senior economist on the Council of Economic Advisers and service as deputy U.S. trade representative under President Bush.
He also worked for several years as a business executive in the private sector at various companies, including Premark International Inc. of Deerfield, Ill.

Moskow holds a bachelor's degree in economics from Lafayette College in Easton, Pa. He also has a master's degree in economics and a PhD in business and applied economics from the University of Pennsylvania.
ROBERT PARRY took office as head of the San Francisco Fed in February 1986.
Parry first joined the U.S. central bank in 1965 as a staff economist at the Fed board in Washington, where he helped build a financial model of the U.S. economy.
He also had a lengthy career at Security Pacific Bank, where he eventually became the bank's chief economist.
Parry holds a bachelor's degree from Gettysburg College and a master's degree and a PhD in economics from the University of Pennsylvania.
